lesson.title: Place value in base 60
lesson.objective: Read whole numbers written in base 60, convert them to base 10, and write base-10 whole numbers as base-60 digit groups.
lesson.approachReason: Fully worked conversions establish the method, then progressively reduced scaffolding lets the learner read and write base-60 numbers independently.

blocks.heading: Two groups, one number
blocks.problem:
Imagine a storekeeper recording a quantity as [2, 15] in base 60. What quantity is that in base 10?

We will use a modern bracket notation: commas separate base-60 digits, each ranging from 0 to 59. These brackets are not Babylonian symbols.

steps.title: Read the rightmost group
steps.why: The rightmost whole-number position has value 1.

steps.title: Read the next group
steps.why: Moving one position left multiplies the place value by 60.

steps.title: Combine the values
steps.why: Add the contribution from each position.

blocks.heading: Each step left is worth 60 times more
blocks.body:
In base 10, whole-number places run from ones to tens to hundreds. In base 60, they run from ones to sixties to 3,600s, because 60 × 60 = 3,600.

Read our bracket notation from right to left to assign those weights: [a, b, c] means a × 3,600 + b × 60 + c. Each group is one base-60 digit, even when we write it using two decimal characters, such as 15.
blocks.example: In this modern notation, a zero keeps a position open: [1, 0] means 1 × 60 + 0 = 60, whereas [1] means 1.

hints: Which group counts ones, and which counts sixties?
Multiply the left group by 60 before adding the right group.
blocks.retry: Think of [3, 4] as three bundles of 60 plus four loose items. The comma separates positions; it does not join the groups into 34.

blocks.heading: Now read three positions
blocks.prompt:
A fictional inventory entry is [1, 2, 3] in base 60. Convert it to base 10.

From left to right, the place values are 3,600, 60, and 1.

traps.feedback: That joins the groups as decimal characters instead of giving each group its base-60 place value.
The leftmost group is worth 3,600, not 60. Each additional position is another factor of 60.

hints: Start with 3,600, then add two sixties and three ones.
blocks.solution: The three contributions are 1 × 3,600 = 3,600; 2 × 60 = 120; and 3 × 1 = 3. Their sum is 3,600 + 120 + 3 = 3,723.

blocks.heading: Run the method backward
blocks.problem: The storekeeper now has 145 items, counted in base 10. Write that quantity in base 60.

steps.title: Choose the largest place needed
steps.text: 145 is less than 3,600 but at least 60, so start with the sixties place.
steps.why: Use the largest place value that fits into the number. A number of at least 3,600 would start with the 3,600s place or a larger place.

steps.title: Count whole sixties
steps.why: The sixties digit is 2: use as many whole sixties as fit.

steps.title: Keep the remainder
steps.why: The leftover amount belongs in the ones place. It is below 60, so it fits in one digit.

steps.title: Write the groups
steps.why: For larger numbers, repeat this process at each smaller place, keeping a zero group if a position contributes nothing.

hints: Every base-60 digit must be between 0 and 59.
Split 65 ones into one group of 60 and five remaining ones.
blocks.retry: A group cannot contain 60 or more in our standard base-60 notation. Exchange 60 ones for one extra sixty, leaving the total unchanged.

blocks.heading: Write the final inventory entry
blocks.prompt:
An inventory contains 7,388 items in base 10. Write this number in base 60 using our bracket notation, such as [a, b, c].

Use the place values 3,600, 60, and 1. Every digit must be between 0 and 59.

traps.feedback: 188 does not fit in one base-60 digit. Also, with only two groups, the left group would count sixties rather than 3,600s.
123 sixties plus 8 ones gives the right total, but 123 exceeds the digit limit. Exchange 120 of those sixties for two groups of 3,600.

hints: First find how many whole groups of 3,600 fit, then subtract their contribution.
Divide the remainder into whole groups of 60 and leftover ones.
blocks.solution: Two groups of 3,600 contribute 2 × 3,600 = 7,200, leaving 7,388 − 7,200 = 188. Three groups of 60 contribute 3 × 60 = 180, leaving 188 − 180 = 8. Therefore the answer is [2, 3, 8]. Check: 7,200 + 180 + 8 = 7,388.

activities.title: Convert 3,674 to base 60
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to convert a fictional stock count of 3,674 into base 60. Work from the largest place value down to the ones.
activities.reveal: 3,674 becomes [1, 1, 14]: 3,600 + 60 + 14 = 3,674. Writing base 60 means separating a total into contributions from successive place values.
steps: Start with the 3,600s place: one group fits, since 1 × 3,600 = 3,600 and 2 × 3,600 = 7,200 is too much.
Use one sixty from the remainder: 74 − 60 = 14.
Write the 3,600s, sixties, and ones digits in order: [1, 1, 14].

questions.question: A storekeeper writes [3, 4] in our base-60 notation. How many items does this represent in base 10?
questions.explanation: The left group counts sixties and the right group counts ones: 3 × 60 + 4 = 180 + 4 = 184.

questions.question: A trainee records 245 items as [3, 65], meaning three sixties plus 65 ones. The total is right, but one digit is too large. Which standard base-60 entry preserves the total?
questions.explanation: Exchange 60 of the 65 ones for one extra sixty, producing four sixties and five ones. Check: 4 × 60 + 5 = 240 + 5 = 245.

problems: The ordering activity supplies all calculations and the final answer, so learners can complete it through procedural sequencing without independently performing a conversion.
The second hint for the digit-normalization check largely gives away the required exchange, reducing the diagnostic value of a retry.
Zero placeholders are explained but never practiced, leaving an important place-value misconception untested.
